candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12: administer medications safely, educate clients about medications, monitor effects and evaluate therapeutic response.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — influenza antiviral timing and medication teaching
candidate.educational_objective: Teach that indicated influenza antiviral therapy should start as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours for greatest benefit, while recognizing that selected hospitalized, severe, progressive, or high-risk patients may benefit even when treatment begins later.

options.A: Start indicated antiviral treatment as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours for greatest benefit; later treatment can still benefit some hospitalized, severe, progressive, or high-risk patients.
options.B: Wait until at least 48 hours have passed because starting influenza antivirals earlier provides less clinical benefit.
options.C: Delay treatment until influenza symptoms are nearly resolved so medication adverse effects are minimized.
options.D: Use timing only for dosing convenience because antiviral treatment benefit is unrelated to illness duration.

candidate.rationale: CDC's March 10, 2026 clinician guidance states that influenza antiviral treatment provides the greatest clinical benefit when started early, especially within 48 hours of illness onset. It also states that treatment can still provide clinical benefit after 48 hours in hospitalized patients and in patients with severe, complicated, or progressive illness; high-risk patients should receive treatment as soon as possible. A is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Influenza antiviral treatment is most beneficial when started as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours, while later treatment may still benefit hospitalized or severe/complicated/progressive illness and treatment is recommended promptly for high-risk patients.
